summary: Defines the architectural framework for Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES), where the parts of a network device that forward packets are separated from the parts that control them. It identifies the entities involved and how they interact. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Think of a router as workers and a boss. This splits them into separate parts that talk to each other, and describes how.

questions: separating control and forwarding in routers
what is the difference between a control element and a forwarding element
what is the fp reference point in forces
subtitle: How a router can be split into separate control and forwarding parts that talk over a standard protocol.

tldr.problem: Inside a router, the parts that make decisions (routing protocols) and the parts that move packets are tied together with proprietary interfaces, so vendors cannot mix and match components.
tldr.mechanism: The ForCES framework names the pieces (Control Elements, Forwarding Elements and their managers), labels the interfaces between them, and describes how a CE and an FE join up and then exchange control messages over one reference point, Fp.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational framework that sets the stage for a separate ForCES Protocol specification; only the Fp interface is in scope for that protocol.

facts.label: Reference points
facts.value: Fp, Fi, Fr, Fc, Ff, Fl

facts.label: Locality targeted first
facts.value: Same box, or at most one local network hop

today: RFC 3746 is an Informational framework, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes the architecture and leaves the ForCES Protocol itself to a separate specification.

sections.title: Why Separate Control from Forwarding
sections.content:
An IP network element (NE), such as a router, NAT, firewall or load balancer, looks like one box from outside. Inside, it has two kinds of parts: control elements (CEs) in the control plane, which run things like routing and signaling protocols, and forwarding elements (FEs) in the forwarding plane, which handle each packet.

ForCES aims to standardize the information exchange between the two planes. The RFC lists the benefits: component vendors can specialize in one part, CEs and FEs from different vendors can interoperate, and capacity can be added without "forklift upgrades". Today's routers with separate blades use proprietary interfaces for CE-FE messaging, and the goal is to replace those with a standard protocol.
sections.eli5: If the planner and the workers speak a common language, you can hire a planner from one company and workers from another and they still get along.

sections.title: Elements, Managers and Reference Points
sections.content:
A ForCES NE may contain several CEs and several FEs. Each FE has physical interfaces to the outside world, and some interconnect (a backplane or a LAN such as Gigabit Ethernet) lets CEs and FEs talk to each other. Two ancillary entities sit outside the NE: the CE Manager and the FE Manager, which configure their CEs and FEs before they associate.

The RFC labels the logical interactions as reference points: Fp (CE-FE), Fi (FE-FE), Fr (CE-CE), Fc (CE Manager to CE), Ff (FE Manager to FE) and Fl (between the two managers). Fi/f is the FE external interface. The ForCES Protocol is defined over only one of these, Fp.

FEs are deliberately simple: they are slaves that only do what CEs tell them. They have no notion of CE redundancy, load sharing or distributed control, so any such coordination is up to the CEs. When several CEs are used, the CEs and FEs together must still look like a single NE.
sections.eli5: The workers only follow orders and never decide who the boss is. The bosses sort that out among themselves, and outsiders just see one kitchen.

sections.title: Pre-association and Post-association Phases
sections.content:
The framework has two operational phases. In the pre-association phase the managers work out which CEs and FEs belong together, using anything from static configuration to a protocol. None of this is within the scope of the ForCES Protocol, and these managers may need to authenticate each other.

In the post-association phase a CE and FE know each other and talk over Fp. Either side can start the connection. The example join sequence is: a security exchange, the FE asks to join, the CE asks what kind of FE it is, the FE describes itself using the FE model, the CE optionally sends initial configuration, and the FE asks to go ahead and the CE agrees. Packet processing cannot begin until the association is established.

In steady state the CE sends instructions such as new routes or statistics queries, and the FE reports events such as a port failure. Because routing packets for the router itself arrive at FEs, the protocol over Fp also carries those data packets to the CE and carries CE-originated packets back out.

The first version targets "very close" CE/FE localities: the same box, or at most one local network hop.
sections.eli5: First someone decides which worker goes with which boss. Then the worker and boss say hello, prove who they are, tell each other what they can do, and only then start working.

sections.title: Restarts and Re-establishing Association
sections.content:
CEs and FEs can join and leave an NE dynamically, and a lost connection can break an association. The framework allows moving back and forth between the two phases, and the protocol should help detect lost association and resynchronize state. Security state must be re-established too, so the same level of authentication and authorization applies afterward.

For a CE graceful restart, the CE tells FEs at association time what to do if it fails. If graceful restart is supported, FEs should keep their state, including forwarding tables, across the restart, and a timer settable by the CE must make that cached state expire eventually. This gives the non-stop forwarding that graceful restart needs.

If an FE leaves or fails, the CE must inform the routing protocols, which likely triggers a recalculation and new forwarding tables for the remaining FEs. A returning FE can rediscover its CE through its FE manager or from cached information, and may use a quick check such as a CRC-32 of its state to avoid resending everything.
sections.eli5: If the boss steps out for a moment, the workers keep doing what they were last told for a short while, so the kitchen does not stop.

sections.title: Fit with the IPv4 Router Requirements
sections.content:
The framework must explain how it supports the router functions in RFC 1812. The general split is that forwarding carries the per-packet work at line speed, while control carries the computationally complex protocols. The RFC admits no rigid line can be drawn, and functions may be offloaded to FEs, as long as they are described in the FE model.

Concretely: IP forwarding by looking up the FIB belongs to FEs, and the FE decrements the TTL by 1 just before sending the packet on. Routing protocols run in CEs, and IGMP is implemented in CEs. For behaviors that could live in either place, such as ARP, CEs MUST be capable of them while FEs MAY implement them. When several FEs process a packet, the NE must still look like one device, so TTL must be decremented only once. Management by SNMP should go through the CE, and AgentX could let the CE act as master agent with FEs as subagents.
sections.eli5: The workers do the quick, repeated jobs, and the bosses handle the tricky thinking. When the workers get strong enough, a few bosses' jobs can be handed down.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Physical separation of CEs and FEs creates a link that may be insecure. The RFC lists threats: flooding a CE with false "join" or "remove" requests, impersonation, replay, attacks during CE fail-over, message injection, eavesdropping, shared keys across many FEs, and denial of service through the external interface. Matching requirements include not creating state until an FE is authenticated, authenticating messages against the list of authorized elements, protecting integrity, and using different security parameters for each FE-CE pair.

Rate limiting MUST be in place at both FE and CE, because a storm of packets arriving on an external interface could overwhelm the CE over Fp. This holds even for a single-box deployment where physical security may let the other mechanisms be turned off.

As ways to meet the needs, the RFC reviews TLS (with reliable transports such as TCP or SCTP) and IPsec (recommending ESP in transport mode, noting replay protection is unavailable with manual key management).
sections.eli5: Because the bosses and workers may be in different rooms, they need a secret handshake, and a guard has to stop a crowd from jamming the boss's door.

items.title: Fp
items.text: CE to FE. The only interface the ForCES Protocol is defined over.

items.text: FE to FE. Carries packets between FEs.

items.title: Fr
items.text: CE to CE. Left to implementations.

items.text: CE Manager to CE, in the pre-association phase.

items.text: FE Manager to FE, in the pre-association phase.
